# Model Comparison and Averaging




Previously we saw that the likelihood ratio test (LRT) is a powerful tool for comparing models. But the LRT has a key restriction: the models being compared must be *nested*---one model must be a simplified version of the other, obtainable by setting some parameters to zero or fixing some free parameters to constants. What happens when the models we want to compare cannot be nested?

Consider a question we left unresolved when studying Poisson GLMs and collinearity: does ***temperature*** or ***human impact*** do a better job predicting tree species richness? We saw that including both in one model runs into collinearity problems because the two predictors are too correlated with each other. So we are left with two competing single-predictor models:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(\mu_\text{nspp}) &= b_0 + b_1 \log(\text{area}) + b_2 \text{ temperature} \\
\log(\mu_\text{nspp}) &= b_0 + b_1 \log(\text{area}) + b_2 \text{ human impact}
\end{aligned}
$$

Neither of these is a special case of the other, and they have the same number of parameters. The LRT cannot help us here. We need a different approach.

## The Akaike Information Criterion

The ***Akaike Information Criterion*** (AIC) is a measure of model support that can be applied to any two models fit to the same data, regardless of whether they are nested:

$$
\text{AIC} = -2\,\mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta}_\text{MLE}) + 2k
$$

where $\mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta}_\text{MLE})$ is the maximum log-likelihood of the model and $k$ is the number of estimated parameters. Lower AIC means better support. We can compute it directly in R with the `AIC` function:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod_temp <- glm.nb(nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c,
                   data = dat_plt)
AIC(mod_temp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2321.152
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mod_hii <- glm.nb(nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + hii,
                  data = dat_plt)
AIC(mod_hii)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2314.374
```


:::
:::


The human impact model has a lower AIC and is therefore better supported by the data.

## Why AIC penalizes more parameters

The $2k$ term in AIC deserves some thought. Why penalize for the number of parameters at all? The reason is that adding parameters to a model will *always* increase the log-likelihood---a model with more parameters can always fit the data at least as well as a simpler one. But fitting the training data better does not necessarily mean making better predictions for new data. A model with too many parameters can ***overfit***: it starts fitting the noise specific to the sample rather than the underlying signal.

We can see the penalty at work when adding a third predictor. The model with both temperature and rainfall has a higher log-likelihood:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod_temp_precip <- glm.nb(
    nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c + rain_annual_mm,
    data = dat_plt
)
logLik(mod_temp_precip)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
'log Lik.' -1143.968 (df=5)
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
logLik(mod_temp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
'log Lik.' -1156.576 (df=4)
```


:::
:::


Yet we should ask whether this improvement is real or just the result of having an extra parameter to absorb noise. The AIC penalty addresses this directly: it incorporates a formal result showing that the expected gap between the log-likelihood on the training data and the log-likelihood on a fresh independent sample of the same size is approximately $k$ parameters. In other words:

$$
\frac{1}{n}\,\mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta} \mid \text{data}_\text{orig}) - \frac{1}{n}\,\mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta} \mid \text{data}_\text{new}) \approx k
$$

So $2k$ (multiplied by the same factor of $-2$ that scales the log-likelihood) adjusts for this systematic optimism, giving a fair comparison across models with different numbers of parameters. When we apply this correction, the `temp + rain` model still comes out ahead:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
AIC(mod_temp_precip)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2297.937
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
AIC(mod_hii)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2314.374
```


:::
:::


We can now be confident that the improvement for the `temp + rain` model is not simply a reward for having one more parameter.

## Interpreting $\Delta$AIC

Because AIC values are only interpretable relative to one another, it is conventional to work with $\Delta\text{AIC}$, the difference between each model's AIC and the minimum AIC in the candidate set. A widely used rule of thumb is that models within 2 AIC units of the best model are effectively equivalent in their support; a difference larger than 2 indicates that one model is genuinely better supported than the other [@burnham-anderson].

## Model averaging

Model comparison tells us which model is best supported---a useful way of testing hypotheses. But sometimes our goal is not to pick a winner and declare the others losers. When the goal is ***prediction***, a different strategy often performs better: ***model averaging***. Rather than relying on a single model, we combine the predictions of multiple models. This can be more accurate than any one model individually, and avoids the problem of pretending there is no uncertainty about which model is correct in the first place.

Consider the three models we have built:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + hii
nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c
nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c + rain_annual_mm
```
:::


Each makes different predictions about the expected species richness of a plot. Combining them is also better than collapsing everything into one big model with all predictors, because we already know that including all predictors together creates collinearity problems, and for smaller data sets it also risks overfitting.

### Averaging the parameters

One natural way to combine models is to average the coefficients. For a variable like temperature that appears in some but not all models, we take the mean of its estimated slopes across all models where it appears:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
coefficients(mod_temp)["avg_temp_annual_c"]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
avg_temp_annual_c 
       0.02427288 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
coefficients(mod_temp_precip)["avg_temp_annual_c"]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
avg_temp_annual_c 
       0.02797484 
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
b31 <- coefficients(mod_temp)["avg_temp_annual_c"]
b32 <- coefficients(mod_temp_precip)["avg_temp_annual_c"]
b3avg <- mean(c(b31, b32))
```
:::


So a simple average slope for temperature would be $b_3^{(\text{avg.})} = \frac{0.024 + 0.028}{2} = 0.026$.

There are actually two conventions for handling variables that do not appear in every model. One averages only over models where the variable appears (as above). The other includes a slope of zero for models that omit the variable, giving a more conservative (smaller) average. The default behavior of the software we will use follows the first convention.

### Weighting by model support

A simple average treats all models equally, but we already know from the AIC values that some models are better supported than others:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
AIC(mod_hii)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2314.374
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
AIC(mod_temp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2321.152
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
AIC(mod_temp_precip)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2297.937
```


:::
:::


It makes sense to give more weight to better-supported models. We do this by converting AIC values into ***Akaike weights***. For model $i$:

$$
w_i = \frac{e^{-\Delta\text{AIC}_i / 2}}{\sum_j e^{-\Delta\text{AIC}_j / 2}}
$$

where $\Delta\text{AIC}_i = \text{AIC}(\text{model}_i) - \min(\text{AIC})$. The weights sum to 1 across all models in the candidate set and can be loosely interpreted as the probability that model $i$ is the best-supported model given the data and the set of models considered.

## Model averaging with the *MuMIn* package

Computing these weights and averaging parameters by hand is tedious. The *MuMIn* package [@mumin] does this for us. The `model.avg` function takes a list of candidate models and returns an averaged model object:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(MuMIn)

mod_avg <- model.avg(list(mod_hii, mod_temp, mod_temp_precip))
```
:::


We can inspect the averaged coefficients directly:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
coefficients(mod_avg)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      (Intercept)    log(Plot_Area) avg_temp_annual_c    rain_annual_mm 
    -2.5267209876      0.4876844180      0.0279748056      0.0000782252 
              hii 
     0.0133591861 
```


:::
:::


The model table, accessed with `$msTable`, shows each candidate model ranked from best to worst supported, along with its AIC, $\Delta$AIC, and weight:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod_avg$msTable
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
    df    logLik     AICc    delta       weight
134  5 -1143.968 2298.052  0.00000 9.997160e-01
23   4 -1153.187 2314.451 16.39911 2.746982e-04
13   4 -1156.576 2321.229 23.17712 9.268898e-06
```


:::
:::


You will notice that *MuMIn* reports AICc rather than AIC. AICc is a sample-size-corrected version of AIC that applies an additional penalty for small samples. It is generally a good idea to prefer AICc; for large samples the correction is negligible:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
AIC(mod_temp_precip)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2297.937
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
AICc(mod_temp_precip)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2298.052
```


:::
:::


## Variable importance via `dredge`

*MuMIn* also provides a function called `dredge` that automatically fits all possible submodels from a global model containing every predictor of interest. Combined with AIC weights, `dredge` can be used to assess the ***relative importance*** of each variable by summing the weights of all models in which that variable appears. Variables that appear in many high-weight models receive a high importance score.

This workflow should be approached with care. Generating every possible combination of predictors and letting AIC pick the winner is a form of data dredging that can inflate false-positive rates and is no substitute for thinking carefully about which variables are biologically meaningful. Indeed, *MuMIn*'s own authors named the function `dredge` as an acknowledgment of this risk. That said, when the candidate variables are pre-selected on biological grounds, summed variable importance scores can provide a useful summary of which predictors are most consistently supported across the model set.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# global model with all predictors of interest
# na.action = "na.fail" is required by dredge
mod_big <- glm.nb(
    nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + hii + avg_temp_annual_c + rain_annual_mm,
    data = dat_plt, na.action = "na.fail"
)

# fit all sub-models and compute AIC weights
big_dredge <- dredge(mod_big)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Fixed term is "(Intercept)"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# summed weights = variable importance
sw(big_dredge)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                     log(Plot_Area) rain_annual_mm hii  avg_temp_annual_c
Sum of weights:      1.00           1.00           0.99 0.45             
N containing models:    8              8              8    8             
```


:::
:::


Plot area is highly important---not a surprise given the well-established species--area relationship. Among the environmental and anthropogenic predictors, human impact index and annual rainfall both receive high summed weights, while temperature is somewhat less consistently supported. This matches the earlier head-to-head comparison where the human impact model outperformed the temperature-only model.
